summary:
Uruguay's trans-protection regime rests on the Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law No. 19684), promulgated by the Executive in October 2018, which establishes state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights and directs government to ensure that trans people are treated respectfully by authorities and are not denied health services.

Legal gender recognition is administrative and based on self-declaration. Since October 2018 no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis has been required to change legal gender on official documents; adults have been able to change name and legal gender since October 2009, and minors may do so with parental consent under the 2018 law. Documents carry only female and male markers, even though article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognises non-binary people in its definitions.

Crimes motivated by sexual orientation or sexual identity attract enhanced penalties under article 149ter of the Penal Code, and incitement to hatred on those grounds has been prohibited since 2003. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created a permanent honorary commission empowered to investigate unlawful discriminatory conduct, including on grounds of sexual orientation and sexual identity. Non-discrimination, a ban on conversion therapy and an equal age of consent of 15 are in force, and hate-crime rules cover sexual orientation and gender identity.

Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, same-sex marriage has been legal since August 2013, and Uruguay was the first country in Latin America to recognise same-sex civil unions, in legislation signed in December 2007 granting couples who had cohabited five years or more rights equivalent to marriage. Joint adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since September 2009, also a regional first.

Trans people in custody have the right to decide whether to be held in a men's or a women's prison. Official figures cited by the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System record 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 people deprived of liberty. The director of the National Rehabilitation Institute told a parliamentary hearing that trans women are currently placed in women's prisons but that cohabitation entails a process of adaptation, and that a new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population; a dedicated sector for trans people was announced in July 2023 as part of a new prison planned for Montevideo.

Lethal and everyday violence against trans people persists. Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder. Studies cited in country coverage report that about two-thirds of transgender Uruguayans have been victims of physical violence and that their life expectancy is around 45 years against a national average of 77.

Discrimination in services is documented in individual cases. In May 2024 a trans health-service user, Andreina Stuart, filed a criminal complaint alleging mistreatment and discrimination at San Carlos hospital in Maldonado, after which the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation and local officials pressed for health-system updates. Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued the state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.
tangentialFactors:
Uruguay is rated Free at 96/100 in Freedom House's 2024 Freedom in the World, with political rights at 40/40 and civil liberties at 56/60, and Outright's country overview of 12 March 2026 records same-sex relations as legal nationwide, legal gender recognition as available and LGBTI organisations as able to register.

Public hostility to the trans law surfaced after its passage. The 2018 statute passed 62-26 in the Chamber of Deputies and 17-12 in the Senate, and between November 2018 and March 2019 about 69,360 signatures were gathered for a pre-referendum against it. Only about 10 percent of voters turned out on 4 August 2019, short of the 25 percent needed to force a vote. The Archbishop of Montevideo has called same-sex adoption a serious error.

Comparative framing is consistently favourable: Uruguay was named the most LGBT-friendly country in Latin America by Americas Quarterly in 2016, about 71 percent of Uruguayans supported same-sex marriage in a 2014 poll, and the country hosted the region's first international LGBT rights conference in July 2016. The gap between statute and practice is acknowledged by officials themselves; the National Rehabilitation Institute director stated that the laws are very advanced in Uruguay but that mentality and infrastructure are not in line.

Social visibility is high, with the Montevideo Pride parade running annually since the 1990s and drawing an estimated 120,000 people in 2018, alongside Punta Pride in Punta del Este each February.
localsOnly:
Law No. 19684 carries material entitlements for residents: a state employment quota for trans people, a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a mandate that trans people receive 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships.

The 2018 law also calls on government to ensure that transgender people are included in housing programmes and are not denied health services. In July 2019 the state water company Obras Sanitarias del Estado began offering jobs to transgender people in compliance with it.

The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis being made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Resident outcomes are weak despite the statutory framework. About 25 percent of transgender Uruguayans left home before the age of 18 following family rejection, 87 percent did not finish secondary school, and other studies indicate roughly 75 percent were expelled from the education system.

From 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men have been able to donate blood under the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending the previous 12-month abstinence requirement, and gay, lesbian and bisexual personnel have served openly in the military since May 2009 under a Defence Minister decree.

Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers.

Unresolved: no non-binary gender marker is issued on official documents despite article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognising non-binary people. Whether any administrative route to a third marker exists is not documented in the available sources.

Unresolved: the criminal complaint against San Carlos hospital filed in May 2024 was still pending at the time of reporting, and the promised administrative investigation was to follow the judicial stage. No outcome is sourced.

Unresolved: Beccah Rivas's allegation that the state bank BROU withheld camera footage and her account of dismissal after publicising the case are allegations in active litigation; no judgment is sourced. The sexual-orientation or gender-identity basis of the guard's conduct as found by a court is likewise not stated.

The dedicated trans sector announced in July 2023 for the new Montevideo prison was estimated by officials to be ready in under two years; completion and current occupancy are not confirmed by the sources. Custody figures date from the 2023 report and are not restated later.
